prompt: Why did Ana lose most of three days on #35?
hint: It was not a question of skill.

choices.text: She chose the wrong programming language
choices.why: Nothing in the story is about the language.

choices.text: The questions were asked too late
choices.why: Right. Each answer arrived after she had built on a guess.
Speed would have built the wrong thing faster.

choices.text: The board had no WIP limit
choices.why: The limit does not make a ticket clear.

prompt: Which belong on a definition of ready? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Yes. Otherwise done is whatever the developer decides.
Yes. A missing payment account is one.
Ready means ready to start, not finished.

choices.text: It is small enough for a few days
choices.why: Yes. If not, it is split first.
A date says when, not what.

prompt: Halfway through a ticket, you find it never said whether to accept Pix. What should you do?
hint: A day asking costs less than two days guessing.

choices.text: Pick the most likely answer and carry on
choices.why: That is the guess the lesson warns against.
Doubles the work, and may still be wrong.

choices.text: Ask, and mark the card blocked
choices.why: Right. Write the question on the ticket and tell whoever owns it.

choices.text: Wait until the review to raise it
choices.why: Then the surprise lands at the end.

prompt: The lesson says #35 Pay online is a wish, not a ticket. Why?

choices.why: Right. No problem, criteria, answers or size.
Any work can be a ticket once it is described.

choices.text: Customers did not ask for it
choices.why: They did; the ticket just does not say so.
The language is not the problem.

prompt: When does refinement look at a ticket?

choices.why: That is too late to shape it.
The review shows finished work.
That is exactly when Ana found the questions.

choices.text: Before anybody is about to start it
choices.why: Right. Near the top of the backlog, ahead of time.

prompt: Why do the three amigos include a tester?
hint: Who asks what happens when it goes wrong?

choices.why: The tester brings questions about behaviour, not wording.

choices.text: They see the unhappy path first
choices.why: Right. Diego would have asked about refunds at once.
The name is a habit, not a rule of Scrum.
Estimating is the whole team's job.

prompt: Which of these tickets are slices of Pay online, not layers? Choose all that apply.
hint: Would a customer understand the title?

choices.why: Yes. A customer can use it on its own.
A layer: nothing a customer can use.
Yes. Complete through every layer.
A layer: only a developer understands the title.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer splitting by slice?
hint: When does the first real feedback arrive?

choices.text: Slices need less code in total
choices.why: The total may be the same; the order differs.
They can; they just cannot be used.
Right. The first slice is used while the next is built.
A slice includes a little of the database.

prompt: How does slicing connect to lesson 9's short branches?
hint: How long does a slice take?

choices.text: A slice fits a one- or two-day branch
choices.why: Right. Big tickets make long branches.

choices.text: Slices need a branch per layer
choices.why: A slice is one branch through every layer.

choices.text: It does not; branches are a Git matter
choices.why: The size of the work decides how long the branch lives.
They are reviewed like any change.

prompt: Why do many teams estimate in points rather than hours?
hint: Bigger or smaller is easier than how long.

choices.why: Scrum does not prescribe a unit.

choices.text: Hours are too precise to add up
choices.why: They add up fine; they are just wrong.

choices.text: People compare sizes better than they predict time
choices.why: Right. And hours turn into deadlines.

choices.text: Points make the team look faster
choices.why: Looking faster is not the purpose.

prompt: A ticket is estimated at 13. What does that usually mean?

choices.why: Points are not days.

choices.text: Too big or unclear: split it
choices.why: Right. It goes back to refinement.

choices.text: It is the most important ticket
choices.why: Size is not importance.
The problem is the ticket, not the hours.

prompt: In planning poker, why does everybody reveal at the same time?
hint: What happens to the second number said aloud?

choices.why: It can make it longer, usefully.

choices.text: So nobody copies the first one
choices.why: Right. A quiet worry weighs as much as a confident guess.

choices.text: So the product owner can vote
choices.why: The people who build and test it vote.
They are shown; the timing is the point.

prompt: The first round is 3, 13, 3, 5. What does the team do?
hint: The odd number may know something.

choices.why: An average hides the refund problem.
The majority can be missing a fact.

choices.text: Let the most senior person decide
choices.why: Seniority does not know about the bank form.

choices.text: Hear the 3 and the 13, then vote again
choices.why: Right. Bruno knew about refunds; the round then agreed on 8.

prompt: A manager wants to compare two teams by their velocity. What is wrong with that?
hint: What is a point relative to?

choices.why: Only within one team, and even then loosely.
It is not secret; it is not comparable.
Right. And once judged, they inflate.
It is the sum of points.

prompt: The usual story point scale is 1, 2, 3, 5, ___, 13.
Put what should have happened to #35 in order.
hint: Estimate what is ready; start what is estimated.
trap: Estimating before splitting puts a 13 on something nobody can size.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The value of estimating is mostly the talk
choices.why: Yes. It found the refund problem.

choices.text: An estimate is a promise about a date
choices.why: It is a size, and a rough one.

choices.text: Some teams plan well with no numbers
choices.why: Yes. They only check each ticket is small.

choices.text: Refinement is only for the product owner
choices.why: Developers and testers bring half the questions.
